questions.q: What is the main advantage of a webhook over polling a security tool's API on a timer?
options: Webhooks never require any authentication at all
Webhooks eliminate the need for HTTPS
Webhooks let the tool push an event the moment it happens, instead of waiting for the next poll and burning API calls on 'nothing changed' checks
Webhooks are only usable for read-only data, never for triggering automation
questions.explain: A webhook flips the model: the sending tool makes an outbound POST the instant something happens, cutting the detection-to-reaction delay and avoiding wasted polling calls.

questions.q: Why does a webhook receiver typically return a quick 202 Accepted instead of doing all downstream work inside the request handler?
options: Most webhook senders use a short timeout and will mark a slow response as failed and retry it, which can cause duplicate processing
202 responses are required by the HTTP specification for all POST requests
A 202 response skips signature verification
Flask cannot return any other status code from a POST route
questions.explain: Senders commonly time out and retry slow endpoints, so receivers accept quickly and push the real work into a separate function or queue.

questions.q: When verifying an inbound webhook's HMAC signature, what must the receiver compute the HMAC over?
options: The re-serialized, parsed JSON object
Only the event_id field
The HTTP response the receiver is about to send back
The raw request body bytes exactly as received, before any JSON parsing
questions.explain: Re-parsing and re-serializing JSON can reorder keys or change whitespace, which would make a signature computed over the raw bytes fail to match even for a legitimate request.

questions.q: Why should signature comparison use hmac.compare_digest() instead of a plain == comparison?
options: == is deprecated in Python 3 and no longer works on strings
compare_digest() runs in constant time, preventing an attacker from using response-timing differences to guess the signature byte by byte
compare_digest() automatically regenerates the shared secret
There is no real difference; either works identically for this purpose
questions.explain: A plain string comparison can short-circuit at the first mismatched byte, leaking timing information; compare_digest() is designed to avoid that side channel.

questions.q: Why is a Python set held in process memory an incomplete solution for tracking already-processed webhook event IDs in production?
options: It resets on every process restart and doesn't share state across multiple running instances of the receiver, so duplicates can still slip through
Sets cannot store string values
Sets automatically expire all entries after exactly one second
Flask does not allow global variables inside a route handler
questions.explain: An in-memory set only tracks state for one running process; a restart or running multiple receiver instances means duplicate events can be reprocessed. A database row or Redis key with a TTL is the production-grade version of the same idea.
